interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is each row move swinging one plane while all three planes still meet at the same dot, when you add a multiple of one row to another until the grid is a staircase.
interactive.title: Clear the columns
interactive.whatAmILookingAt:
Thirteen small screens share one picture. On top is the grid: three rows, one for each equation. The letters x, y and z head columns 1 to 3. A bar marks off a fourth column, the constants. Below it is a 3-D view of three planes, one for each row. Each plane carries its row's number. Dragging the background turns the view. A dot marks the answer, where all three planes meet. Its x, y and z read out.

The rule. Each equation in x, y and z is a flat plane. A row move adds a multiple of one row to another. A point that fits both rows fits the new one. Taking the same multiple away brings the old row back. So no new point gets in either. Every point where the two planes cross fits the new row. So the changed row's plane swings about that line. The dot sits on that line, so it stays put. Clear column 1 below row 1, then column 2 below row 2. The grid is then a staircase, with zeros under its diagonal. Its bottom row gives z. Then row 2 gives y, and row 1 gives x.

The screens.
- 1, the grid and the planes. The grid holds x + y + z = 6, 2x + y − z = 1 and x − y + 2z = 5, as [1 1 1 | 6; 2 1 −1 | 1; 1 −1 2 | 5]. The three planes rise into view one at a time. The dot settles where all three meet, at (1, 2, 3). This plays once as the screen opens. Its still shows the three planes and the dot, read as: each equation in x, y and z is a flat plane. Each one also makes one row of the grid. The last column holds the constant. The answer is the point where all three planes meet, here (1, 2, 3).
- 2, a puzzle. Which row is x − 2z = 5? The choices are [1 0 −2 | 5], [1 −2 0 | 5] and [1 −2 | 5]. Picking [1 −2 0 | 5] gets the hint: column 2 is for y. The −2 belongs to z, in column 3. Picking [1 −2 | 5] gets the hint: every row needs a place for x, y and z. A missing letter gets a 0. After Check, the row lines up under the grid's x, y and z. Its 0 sits under y.
- 3, a row move. Row 2 lights up. Row 1, times −2, slides down onto it. It adds in, entry by entry. Row 2 becomes [0 −1 −3 | −11]. Plane 2 swings round and still passes through the dot. This plays once as the screen opens. Then the move is yours. You pick the row to change and the row to add. The multiplier runs from −3 to 3, skipping 0. Add makes the move, and Reset brings back the first grid. Every move swings one plane. The dot stays put. Its still shows plane 2 swung round through the dot, read as: a row move adds a multiple of one row to another. Here −2 × row 1 goes into row 2. Row 2 becomes 0, −1, −3 and −11. Plane 2 swings about the line it shares with plane 1. So it still passes through the dot at (1, 2, 3).
- 4, a puzzle. Add −1 × row 1 to row 3. What does row 3 become? The choices are [0 −2 1 | −1], [0 −2 1 | 5] and [2 0 3 | 11]. Picking [0 −2 1 | 5] gets the hint: the constant column changes too. Picking [2 0 3 | 11] gets the hint: that adds row 1. −1 lots of row 1 takes it away. After Check, row 3 becomes [0 −2 1 | −1]. Plane 3 swings round through the dot. Column 1 is now clear below row 1.
- 5, the staircase. Row 2, times −2, adds into row 3. Row 3 becomes [0 0 7 | 21]. A staircase line is drawn under the grid's diagonal. Then the answers fill in from the bottom. 7z = 21 gives z = 3. Then −y − 9 = −11 gives y = 2, and x + 2 + 3 = 6 gives x = 1. This plays once as the screen opens. Its still shows the finished staircase and the answers, read as: add −2 × row 2 to row 3, and the grid becomes a staircase. It has zeros under its diagonal. Read it from the bottom up: 7z = 21, so z = 3. Then −y − 9 = −11 gives y = 2. Last, x + 2 + 3 = 6 gives x = 1.
- 6, a puzzle. The staircase [2 1 −1 | 3; 0 3 1 | 5; 0 0 2 | 4] is finished. What is x? The choices are 2, 0 and 1. Picking 0 gets the hint: row 1's z entry is −1, so its z term is −2, not +2. Picking 1 gets the hint: row 1 has a z term too. Put in z as well as y. After Check, the answers fill in from the bottom: z = 2, y = 1 and x = 2.
- 7, no common point. A new grid loads: x + y + z = 3, x − y + z = 1 and 2x + 2z = 9, as [1 1 1 | 3; 1 −1 1 | 1; 2 0 2 | 9]. Three moves play. −1 × row 1 into row 2 gives [0 −2 0 | −2]. −2 × row 1 into row 3 gives [0 −2 0 | 3]. −1 × row 2 into row 3 gives [0 0 0 | 5]. Each pair of planes crosses along a line. The three lines run side by side, and no dot appears. This plays once as the screen opens. Its still shows the three planes and their three lines, read as: a new grid, x + y + z = 3, x − y + z = 1 and 2x + 2z = 9. Its bottom row ends up 0 = 5. No point can fit that, so there is no answer. No two of these planes are parallel. Each pair crosses along a line, but the three lines run side by side and never meet.
- 8, a puzzle. Row 3's constant changes from 9 to 4, so row 3 reads 2x + 2z = 4. The same three moves run. What constant ends the bottom row? The choices are 0, 5 and 4. Picking 5 gets the hint: that was for 9. Run the moves on the new constant. Picking 4 gets the hint: the moves change the constant too. Take 2 × 3 away, then take away −2. After Check, plane 3 slides across. The bottom row reads [0 0 0 | 0]. All three planes now pass through one line.
- 9, a whole line. The grid from screen 8 stays, ending [0 0 0 | 0]. The shared line is drawn. A dot on it reads out x, y and z. A slider for t runs the dot along the line, from −2 to 2 in steps of 0.5. At every t, the dot's point fits all three equations. Its still is set at t = 1, with the dot on (1, 1, 1), read as: the bottom row now says 0 = 0, which every point fits. That is because row 3 is row 1 plus row 2. All three planes share the line where planes 1 and 2 cross. Each number t picks one point on it: x = 2 − t, y = 1 and z = t. At t = 1 that is (1, 1, 1).
- 10, a puzzle. The grid [1 2 −1 | 4; 2 1 1 | 5; 3 3 0 | 9] has a determinant of 0. Before the moves run, how many answers will it have? The choices are none, exactly one, and a whole line of them. Check runs the three moves, and the grid steps down to [1 2 −1 | 4; 0 −3 3 | −3; 0 0 0 | 0]. Picking none gets the hint: the moves end 0 = 0, and every point fits that. Picking exactly one gets the hint: no row is left to pin down z, so z is free. After a right answer, the three planes swing into view, sharing one line. A dot runs along it.
- 11, the circuit. Three loops sit in a row above the grid, in place of the planes. The loop currents I₁, I₂ and I₃ are drawn clockwise. Each end loop has 3 Ω of its own and the middle loop 6 Ω. Each pair of neighbours shares 3 Ω. 12 V drives loop 1 and 6 V drives loop 3. The grid [6 −3 0 | 12; −3 12 −3 | 0; 0 −3 6 | 6] reads out. Row 2 doubles, then row 1 adds in. Row 2 becomes [0 21 −6 | 12]. This plays once as the screen opens. Its still shows the circuit and the grid after the move, read as: three loops sit in a row. These are example figures. Each end loop has 3 Ω of its own and the middle loop 6 Ω. Each pair of neighbours shares 3 Ω. 12 V drives loop 1 and 6 V drives loop 3. Going round each loop gives one row: 6I₁ − 3I₂ = 12, −3I₁ + 12I₂ − 3I₃ = 0 and −3I₂ + 6I₃ = 6. Down the diagonal is each loop's total resistance. Off it is minus what two loops share. Double row 2 and add row 1. Multiplying a row by any number but 0 is safe. Here it turns the −3 into −6, which row 1's 6 clears. Row 2 becomes 0, 21, −6 and 12.
- 12, a mixed puzzle. Row 2 is now [0 21 −6 | 12], and row 3 is still [0 −3 6 | 6]. Which move clears the −3 in row 3, column 2? The choices are 7 × row 3, plus row 2; row 3 plus row 2; and 2 × row 3, plus row 1. Picking row 3 plus row 2 gets the hint: that leaves 18 in column 2, not 0. Picking 2 × row 3, plus row 1 gets the hint: row 1 puts a 6 back in column 1. Use row 2, which has a 0 there. After Check, row 3 becomes [0 0 36 | 54]. The currents fill in from the bottom. I₃ = 54 ÷ 36 = 1.5 A. Then 21I₂ − 9 = 12 gives I₂ = 1 A. Then 6I₁ − 3 = 12 gives I₁ = 2.5 A. The resistor that loops 2 and 3 share shows I₂ − I₃ = −0.5 A. Its arrow shows 0.5 A, against loop 2's arrow.
- 13, a mixed puzzle. The grid [1 1 1 | 3; 1 2 3 | 6; 2 3 4 | 10] has a determinant of 0. Clear column 1, then column 2. What does the bottom row say? The choices are 0 = 1, so no answer; 0 = 0, so a whole line; and z = 1, so exactly one. Picking 0 = 0 gets the hint: the x, y and z entries cancel, but the constants leave 4 − 3 = 1. Picking z = 1 gets the hint: a zero determinant rules out exactly one answer. After Check, the working shows [0 1 2 | 3], then [0 1 2 | 4], then [0 0 0 | 1]. The planes cross in pairs along three lines that never meet.

Some screens show an idea. The rest ask you to try it. Each puzzle offers three choices. On a narrow phone they wrap onto more lines. No word splits. The row pickers, the multiplier and Add also wrap at 360 px. A wrong pick is drawn too, so you can see where it goes wrong.
interactive.ignores: Each plane is drawn as a square patch, but it runs on for ever in every direction. The 3-D view is drawn on a flat screen, so some lengths look shorter than they are. The readouts give the true values. The circuit is ideal, with fixed resistances and no wire resistance. Its values are example figures. Every grid here keeps to whole numbers so the working stays short. Real ones rarely do. A calculator or computer runs the same moves on them.

explain.text:
Three equations in three unknowns can be solved in one sweep on a grid. Write each equation as a row, with x, y and z in columns 1 to 3 and the constant in a fourth column. A missing letter gets a 0. Each equation in x, y and z is also a flat plane in space. The answer is the point where all three planes meet. That is the dot in the picture. [[Gaussian elimination]] steps the grid down to a staircase, with zeros under its diagonal. The answer stays the same. Then you solve it from the bottom row up.

The tool is the row move: add a multiple of one row to another.[^1] It is the stack, scale and add move you already use, done on a grid. Here is why it never changes the answer. Say a point fits row 1 and row 2. Then each row's two sides are equal. Add equal amounts to equal amounts and they stay equal. So the point fits the new row too. Take the same multiple away again and the old row comes back. So the move lets in no new answers either. In the picture, every point where planes 1 and 2 cross fits the new row. So plane 2 swings about that line. The dot sits on that line, so it stays put. Multiplying a row by any number but 0 is safe for the same reason. Multiplying by 0 would wipe the row out. Nothing could bring it back.

Take x + y + z = 6, 2x + y − z = 1 and x − y + 2z = 5. Add −2 × row 1 to row 2, and row 2 becomes 0, −1, −3 and −11. Add −1 × row 1 to row 3, and row 3 becomes 0, −2, 1 and −1. Column 1 is now clear below the top. Add −2 × row 2 to row 3, and row 3 becomes 0, 0, 7 and 21. The grid is a staircase. Its bottom row says 7z = 21, so z = 3. Row 2 says −y − 3z = −11, so −y − 9 = −11 and y = 2. Row 1 says x + y + z = 6, so x + 2 + 3 = 6 and x = 1. Working up like this is [[back-substitution]]. Put (1, 2, 3) back into the first three equations, not the stepped ones. They give 6, 1 and 5, as they should.

The finished grid also says how many answers there are. Three equations can have exactly one answer, infinitely many, or none. A bottom row of 0, 0, 0 and 5 says 0 = 5. No point fits that, so there is no answer. The planes need not be parallel for that. In the picture they cross in pairs along three lines that never meet. A bottom row of 0, 0, 0 and 0 says 0 = 0. Every point fits that. That row adds no limit. In the picture the other two planes meet along a line. Every point on that line fits all three equations. Both of those grids have a determinant of 0. A zero determinant rules out exactly one answer. Only the finished grid says whether there are none or many. Elimination is also the last step in solving the three-loop circuit. Going round each loop gives one equation in the loop currents.[^2] This works only for a circuit you can draw flat, with no wires crossing. Elimination then finds all three at once.

Real systems are far bigger. A computer solves them, often with these same row moves. A ship's power network is written as a grid called the bus admittance matrix.[^3] A reactor core code builds one large grid for the core and hands it to a solver.[^4] You may also meet Cramer's rule. It finds each unknown as a ratio of two determinants. When the determinant is 0, it cannot tell none from many. The inverse of a 3 by 3 matrix comes from the same row moves, or from a calculator. Linear algebra takes all this further, with inverses by hand, rank, pivots and the fully reduced grid.

**Row moves step three equations down to a staircase with the same answer. Back-substitution then solves it from the bottom up. A row reading 0 = 5 means no answer. With no such row, a row of 0 = 0 means infinitely many.**

analogy.text: Think of three cores in a cable, linked at the far end. You can only read two at a time, in series. Say you read 0.9 Ω for cores a and b, 0.7 Ω for b and c, and 0.8 Ω for a and c. Take the second reading from the first, and b drops out: a − c = 0.2 Ω. Add the third, and c drops out: 2a = 1.0 Ω, so a = 0.5 Ω. Then b = 0.4 Ω and c = 0.3 Ω. Each combined reading is still true, just as each row move keeps the answer.
analogy.breaks: Real readings carry meter error and lead resistance. Combining them adds the errors up. A grid's numbers are exact. A core cannot have a negative resistance. An answer from a grid can be negative, like a loop current that flows the other way.

practice.text:
- Write each equation as a row: x, y and z in columns 1 to 3, the constant last. Put a 0 for a missing letter.
- Use row 1 to clear column 1 in rows 2 and 3: add a multiple of row 1 to each.
- Use the new row 2 to clear column 2 in row 3. Row 1 would put a number back in column 1.
- If the row you clear with has a 0 in that column, first swap it with a lower row that does not. A swap is safe: the equations stay the same, just in a new order.
- Read the rows. Any row of 0 = a number other than 0 means no answer. With no such row, a row of 0 = 0 means infinitely many. Otherwise the bottom row gives z.
- Work up: put z into row 2 to find y, then y and z into row 1 to find x.
- Check the answer in the first equations, not the stepped ones.

**Rules of thumb:** Do to the constant whatever you do to the rest of the row. To keep whole numbers, multiply a row by a number other than 0 before you add. A determinant that is not 0 means exactly one answer. A determinant of 0 means none or many, and only the finished grid says which.

**Worked example:** Three loops sit in a row. Each end loop has 3 Ω of its own, and the middle loop 6 Ω. Each pair of neighbours shares 3 Ω. 12 V drives loop 1 and 6 V drives loop 3. These are example figures. Draw all three loop currents clockwise. Going round each loop then gives 6I₁ − 3I₂ = 12, −3I₁ + 12I₂ − 3I₃ = 0 and −3I₂ + 6I₃ = 6. The grid's determinant is 324, so there is exactly one answer. Double row 2 and add row 1: 21I₂ − 6I₃ = 12. Multiply row 3 by 7 and add the new row 2: 36I₃ = 54, so I₃ = 1.5 A. Then 21I₂ − 9 = 12, so I₂ = 1 A. Then 6I₁ − 3 = 12, so I₁ = 2.5 A. Check in row 2 of the first grid: −7.5 + 12 − 4.5 = 0. The resistor that loops 2 and 3 share carries I₂ − I₃ = −0.5 A. So 0.5 A flows through it against loop 2's arrow.

**Common mistakes**
- Leaving the constant column out of a move.
- Putting a number in the wrong column when a letter is missing.
- Clearing column 2 with row 1. That spoils the zero in column 1.
- Reading 0 = 0 as no answer. On its own it means many answers.
- Reading a zero determinant as no answer. It can mean many.
- Checking only in the stepped grid. A slip in a move then goes unseen.

interactive.html:
On top, a grid of three equations. Below it, the three flat planes they make in 3-D, and later a circuit with example values.

A row move never changes the answer, and the finished grid says how many answers there are.
interactive.title: Clear the columns
interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is each row move swinging one plane while all three planes still meet at the same dot, when you add a multiple of one row to another until the grid is a staircase.

checks.label: Add a nonzero multiple of one row to another row: on the row-move screen every pick of two different rows and a nonzero multiplier changes that one row, swings its plane about the line it shares with the added row's plane, and leaves the dot where it was

The equations are replaced by a system having the same solution but in triangular form, then solved by back-substitution: the staircase screen ends with zeros under the diagonal and the first grid's answer, and its lines find z, then y, then x

A system may have a unique solution, an infinity of solutions or no solution at all: the first planes meet at one dot; the grid whose bottom row ends as zero equals a number other than zero has no dot and three side-by-side lines; the grid whose bottom row is all zeros has a shared line, every point of which fits

Breaking the circuit into simple loops leads to a set of linear equations in the unknown currents: each loop's row holds its total resistance on the diagonal and minus each shared resistance beside it, and the currents found fit every first row

Every worked number is right: −2 × row 1 makes row 2 [0 −1 −3 | −11]; −1 × row 1 makes row 3 [0 −2 1 | −1] (5 and 11 are the slips); −2 × row 2 makes [0 0 7 | 21], so z = 3, y = 2 and x = 1, and (1, 2, 3) gives 6, 1 and 5; the staircase puzzle gives (2, 1, 2), with 0 and 1 the slips; the grid ending 9 steps to 0 = 5 and the one ending 4 to 0 = 0, both with determinant 0; the line is (2 − t, 1, t); the third grid steps to [0 −3 3 | −3] and 0 = 0; the circuit's determinant is 324, row 2 becomes [0 21 −6 | 12] and row 3 [0 0 36 | 54], giving 1.5 A, 1 A and 2.5 A, with −7.5 + 12 − 4.5 = 0 and 0.5 A against loop 2 (18 and 6 are the slips); the last grid ends 0 = 1
Each puzzle's answer comes from the rule, and each wrong answer offered is the slip its hint names
Each puzzle offers three different answers, accepts only the right one, and draws every wrong one in the warning colour
Before Check, no puzzle shows its answer; after a right answer, it does
On the line screen, at every t the slider can take, the dot sits at (2 − t, 1, t) on the shared line, and putting it into each first equation gives back that equation's constant

Each demonstration ends where the lesson says: the first planes meet at (1, 2, 3); row 2 becomes [0 −1 −3 | −11] with the dot unmoved; the grid ending 9 has no dot; the circuit's row 2 becomes [0 21 −6 | 12]

Where the three planes never meet, the view looks about 30 degrees off their lines, so they show as a triangle, not as stacked squares; where they share a line, about 50 degrees off it, so the line stays long
Every demonstration has finished arriving within its 3 to 5 s, none starting before the 0.35 s screen fade ends; every answer's motion, right or wrong, within 3 s

applied.problem: The steps fail as written when a clearing row has 0 in its own column (e.g. an equation with no x put first): no multiple of it clears anything. Textbooks list swapping two rows as a row operation that fixes this.
